title: Highland cattle
wiki_lead: The Highland (Scottish Gaelic: Bò Ghàidhealach) (Scots: Hieland Kye) is a Scottish breed of cattle. It originated in the Scottish Highlands and the Western Islands of Scotland and has long horns and a long shaggy coat. It is a hardy breed – often referred to as 'rustic' – able to withstand the intemperate conditions in the region. The first herd-book dates from 1885; two types – a smaller island type, usually black, and a larger mainland type, usually dun – were registered as a single breed. It is reared primarily for beef, and has been exported to several other countries.
wiki_excerpt:
The Highland (Scottish Gaelic: Bò Ghàidhealach) (Scots: Hieland Kye) is a Scottish breed of cattle. It originated in the Scottish Highlands and the Western Islands of Scotland and has long horns and a long shaggy coat. It is a hardy breed – often referred to as 'rustic' – able to withstand the intemperate conditions in the region. The first herd-book dates from 1885; two types – a smaller island type, usually black, and a larger mainland type, usually dun – were registered as a single breed. It is reared primarily for beef, and has been exported to several other countries.


History

The Highland is a traditional breed of western Scotland. There were two distinct types. The Kyloe, reared mainly in the Hebrides or Western Islands, was small and was frequently black. The cattle were so called because of the practice of swimming them across the narrow straits or kyles separating the islands from the mainland. The cattle of the mainland were somewhat larger and very variable in colour; they were often brown or red.
These cattle were important to the Scottish economy of the eighteenth century. At markets such as those of Falkirk or Crieff, many were bought by drovers from England, who moved them south over the Pennines to be fattened for slaughter. In 1723, over 30000 Scottish cattle were sold into England.
A breed society was established in 1884, and in 1885 published the first volume of the herd-book. In this, the two types were recorded without distinction as 'Highland'.
In 2002, the number of registered breeding cows in the United Kingdom was about 2500; by 2012, this had risen to some 6000. In 2021, it was 3161; the conservation status of the breed in the United Kingdom is listed in DAD-IS as endangered/at risk. The number of unregistered cattle is not known. 
Although a group of cattle is generally called a herd, a group of Highland cattle is known as a "fold". This is because in winter, the cattle were kept in open stone shelters called folds to protect them from the weather at night. 
In 1954, Queen Elizabeth II decided to keep a herd of Highland cattle at Balmoral Castle where they are still kept today.

From the late nineteenth century, stock was exported to various countries, among them Argentina, Australia, Canada, the Falkland Islands, the former Soviet Union, and the United States. Later in the twentieth century, there were exports to various European countries. In 2022, the breed was reported to DAD-IS by twenty-three countries, of which seventeen reported population data. The total population world-wide was reported at just over 40000, with the largest numbers in France and Finland.


Australia
Scottish immigrants brought small numbers of cattle to Australia from the mid-nineteenth century, but by the late 1800s, none remained. Re-establishment of the breed began with an import of two cows and a bull from Scotland in 1954. grok_lead: Highland cattle are a hardy breed of beef cattle originating from the Scottish Highlands, characterized by their distinctive long, curved horns, shaggy double-layered coats in colors such as red, black, yellow, dun, white, and brindle, and robust build adapted to harsh, rugged environments through centuries of natural selection. The breed's history traces back to at least the 12th century, with archaeological evidence suggesting even earlier presence in Scotland, where two main strains developed: the smaller, black Kyloe cattle from the western islands and larger, reddish cattle from the mainland Highlands. These strains merged over time into the modern Highland breed, with the first herd book established by the Highland Cattle Society in 1884. First imported to North America in the 1880s, Highland cattle gained popularity for improving herd hardiness, leading to the formation of the American Highland Cattle Association in 1948 to preserve pedigrees and promote the breed. Physically, mature Highland cows typically weigh 900 to 1,300 pounds with a withers height around 42 to 48 inches, while bulls range from 1,500 to 2,000 pounds and stand slightly taller; both sexes exhibit long horns, with cows featuring upward-sweeping arcs and bulls having thicker, horizontal horns with upturned tips. Their iconic long outer coat, which can reach 13 inches, combined with a soft undercoat, provides exceptional insulation against extreme cold and wet conditions, allowing them to thrive without excessive body fat and enabling efficient foraging on poor-quality pastures, brush, and even woody plants. Known for their docile, even-tempered nature and high intelligence, Highland cattle are easily halter-trained and exhibit strong maternal instincts, longevity, and resistance to diseases and parasites, making them well-suited to diverse climates from the Scottish moors to arid regions like Texas or cold areas like Alaska. Primarily raised for beef production, their meat is prized for its lean quality, marbling, and rich flavor, often commanding premium prices, while their browsing habits also make them valuable for conservation grazing to control invasive plants and improve land management. The breed is considered secure, with over 25,000 registered animals worldwide and annual U.S. registrations exceeding 1,000 as of 2019, reflecting its enduring appeal and successful adaptation beyond its native origins.
